The Gadarene Demoniac
GAD-uh-reen dih-MOH-nee-ak
noun (Gospel narrative)
From Gadarene, of the region of Gadara east of Galilee; demoniac from Greek daimonizomenos, one possessed by demons.

Biblical Definition

The Gadarene demoniac is the man, recorded chiefly in Mark 5:1-20 (with Matt 8 and Luke 8), who dwelt among the tombs in the country of the Gadarenes, possessed by a legion of unclean spirits and so fierce that no chains could bind him. He had "his dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with chains" (Mark 5:3), and night and day he cried and cut himself with stones. When Jesus came, the unclean spirit, asked his name, answered, "My name is Legion: for we are many" (Mark 5:9), and the demons besought leave to enter a herd of swine, whereupon "the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea" and perished (Mark 5:13). The men of the country came and found him "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mark 5:15), a living monument of Christ's power to deliver. The Lord then sent him home to publish how great things God had done for him. The accounts speak of Gadara and of Gergesa, neighboring places of the same region named with differing precision, no contradiction but the ordinary breadth of a district's name. This dictionary confesses the narrative as sober history, displaying Christ's absolute sovereignty over the powers of darkness and His mercy in restoring a man whom the demons had wholly undone.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Gadarene demoniac is the man of Mark 5 who dwelt among the tombs, possessed by a legion of unclean spirits whom Christ cast into the swine. Afterward he sat clothed and in his right mind, a monument of deliverance. The Gadara and Gergesa references name the same region with differing precision.

GADARENE DEMONIAC, noun. The man of the Gadarene country, possessed by a legion of unclean spirits, whom Christ delivered.

He dwelt among the tombs, untamable and self-wounding, until the Lord cast the demons into the swine.

"And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mark 5:15).

His deliverance displays Christ's sovereign authority over the powers and His mercy toward the wretched.

Restored, he was sent home to publish how great things the Lord had done for him.

Key Scripture

Mark 5:9 — "And he asked him, What is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name is Legion: for we are many."

Mark 5:13 — "And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea."

Mark 5:15 — "And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid."

Luke 8:35 — "Then they went out to see what was done; and came to Jesus, and found the man, out of whom the devils were departed, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid."

Modern Corruption

Critics seize on the Gadara and Gergesa references to allege a geographical contradiction, and naturalists explain the possession away as mere madness rather than real demonic bondage.

expand to see more

Skeptics point to the naming of Gadara, Gergesa, and the Gerasenes across the Gospel manuscripts and parallels as proof of error, but this is no contradiction. Gadara was a chief city of the district, Gergesa a nearer town by the lakeshore, and the region could be named by either with differing precision, much as one might place an event near a county or near its principal town. The Evangelists report the same true event from the same region. Likewise the naturalist who reduces the man's state to insanity must explain away the intelligent speech of the demons, their bargaining, and their entrance into the swine.

Recover the narrative as sober history and rich gospel. Here is a man wholly mastered by a legion of spirits, beyond all human help, whom Christ restores with a word, leaving him clothed and in his right mind at the Master's feet. The account magnifies the Lord's absolute dominion over the powers of darkness and His tender mercy toward the most ruined of sinners, and ends with the delivered man sent home to testify.

Hebrew Roots

Gadarene names the region of Gadara, and demoniac renders Greek daimonizomenos, one possessed by demons.

expand to see more

Gadarene derives from Gadara, a chief city of the Decapolis east of the Sea of Galilee.

Gergesa, the reading in some accounts, names a nearer lakeside town within the same district.

Greek daimonizomenos, demonized, supplies the English demoniac, one held by evil spirits.

Legion renders the Latin legio, a Roman unit of thousands, marking the multitude of the demons.

The phrase "in his right mind" (sophronounta) names the soundness Christ restored to the man.

Usage

"The Gadarene demoniac, once untamable among the tombs, sat clothed and in his right mind at Christ's feet."

"He showed that the Gadara and Gergesa references name one region, not a contradiction in the Gospels."

"Legion cast into the swine displays Christ's utter dominion over the demonic powers."
